dct_description_sm:
Wildlife Attractant Bylaw Violations | Squamish Community Dashboard

This indicator tracks the annual number of District of Squamish Wildlife Attractant Bylaw Offence Notices (BONs) and Notices of Infractions (NOIs) issued per year in relation to improperly stored attractants. The number of Wildlife Attractant BONs and NOIs provides insights into attractant availability and guides educational and awareness efforts. While this indicator does not provide an absolute representation of human-wildlife conflicts, it is an important component to assess both successes and areas for improvement. By using proactive bylaw enforcement management, communities can reduce conflicts between humans and bears by identifying and eliminating the root causes of the conflicts.

About this target:

Progressively reduce the availability of wildlife attractants through community-wide education and enforcement of the Wildlife Attractant Bylaw.

Analysis:

In 2024, the District issued 151 Wildlife Attractant BONs (notices) and 109 NOIs (warnings). Over the last several years, the Bylaw Department has increased education in high densified areas where reminder letters are left at the properties, with subsequent inspections for compliance, until compliance is achieved. Bylaw Officers also worked in partnership with communication from the Conservation Officers in the Squamish Area. The team’s enforcement was also driven by public complaints for bear activity in any given area within the District of Squamish’s jurisdiction.

In 2021, the District issued 53 Wildlife Attractant BONs (notices) and 30 NOIs (warnings). This was a notable increase over reported notices and warnings issued in 2020 (8 notices, and 9 warnings) reflecting significantly improved resourcing following the restrictions imposed by and the social and financial impacts of COVID-19 in 2019/2020. The year previous (2018), increased resources were devoted to proactive wildlife attractant audits, as reflected in the number of BONs and NOIs.

Reason for monitoring:

Proactive education along with enforcement efforts are effective in increasing compliance and may lead to greater resident behaviour change resulting in fewer human-wildlife conflicts, property damage, and the number of bears relocated or destroyed. The primary goal of the Bear Smart Program is to reduce the potential for human-bear conflicts and the District of Squamish remains committed to maintaining its Bear Smart status. Education and enforcement efforts assist with motivating residents to make the necessary changes to reduce the frequency and intensity of human-wildlife conflicts and contribute to decreasing property damage and the number of preventable bear relocations and destructions.
